utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the Court permits, I would like to raise a small matter before we again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived here, I had expected to testify earlier in the week and I had agreed to give a lecture in Amsterdam on Friday afternoon at 3.00. This is now Friday, and if there is any chance we can finish earlier than that, I could still make it to Amsterdam. Otherwise, I need to notify the organisers. I understand that my first obligation is to the court and to the interests of justice, but I'd like to know whether to notify them to cancel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Having heard that, we'll reduce the time for lunch break to half an hour from an hour, and we can -- we can conclude at least by 2.30, and I don't think Mr. Karadzic would need all those time. He is going to spend about three hours for your cross, so I'm confident we can conclude around by 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see. Before we begin and without having to going -- go into private session, I will just term it in general terms, but I wonder, Mr. Tieger, then whether Prosecution is prepared to respond to the motion by the accused which relates to certain Rule 70 conditions. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. President, but in any event, let me -- I -- do you have a time-frame, a particular time-frame in mind and I can get back to the Court shortly on the status and progress of the Prosecution's position on that? But it would be helpful if I knew that you had a particular time-frame in mind rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we would like to deal with it -- we have to deal with it in the absence of the witness. The motion I referred to was filed on 8th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, good morning. And I'm certainly not going to take half an hour with the next slide which is what I intimated to you at the end of the session yesterday. I apologise. I was jumping ahead and I thought you meant how long I was going to take to complete Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony -- evidence in chief, that is. And we're also assisted today by Ms. Janet Stewart in Mr. Reid's absence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So we will finish where we were -- left off on the last slide of the -- when we were dealing, Mr. Riedlmayer, with some of the characteristics of the destruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I if could have 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, briefly, I wonder whether Ms. Pelic has been officially introduced?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, she has, Your Honour, but not in open session. So we are assisted also today by Ms. Lena Pelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 65 ter number 23553, please. If we could go to slide number 11, which is page number 11 of e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, what's the significance of the photograph's that we now have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a mosque in the town of Kozarac in Prijedor municipality. It's the Mutnik mosque. It's a considerably old and prominent building. As we saw in the slides yesterday, the most prominent landmark is the minaret which you see in the pre-war photograph on the right. The photograph at the left was taken after the war at a 90 degree angle from -- clockwise from the pre-war photo, and you can see the minaret is missing. The building has been completely burned out, and it's also worth noting that this is a building that stands at some distance from the main street on a small rise. So it's not likely to have gotten into the way of other kinds of attacks. I think whatever happened to it happened to it specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were some categories of buildings more heavily damaged or destroyed than others?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I observe in my report, the old and prominent mosques, the ones dating back to the Ottoman and Austrian period and especially the listed monuments, the ones under special legal protection suffered a higher percentage of damage than others did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the next slide, please. This is, I think, your first of two examples. Can you describe what's seen in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Aladza mosque in Foca. It was a protected monument. It dates from the 16th century. The photo at left is a pre-war photo. The photo at right was taken in 1996 after the end of the war, and you can see that not only has the mosque been destroyed but the rubble has also been removed. All that is still visible is the outlines of the foundation and that circular pattern in front is the foundation of the ablution fountain which you can see on the right in the pre-war photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May we go to the next slide. Now, I think there are three slides relating to this example.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe what's shown in this first slide.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the mosque of Sultan Mehmed the conqueror on top of a hundred metre high cliff at Kuslat at the southern portion of Zvornik municipality. It is reputing to be one of the oldest mosques in Bosnia and it was a protected monument, listed by legislative protection. This is a pre-war view from the institute for the protection of monuments looking down into the valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the next slide?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At left is another photo taken before the war by the institute for protection of monuments. You can see the mosque sitting on the cliff. The photo at right was taken in May of 2002. It does not show a mosque. If you look very carefully, the peak at the left of the top of the cliff is where the mosque used to be. During my survey, I passed by here and looked for the mosque, did not see it. I inquired about going up there, and was told that it was a two-hour climb and it would take the rest of the day. So I did not actually go up there but recorded the absence of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2006 I acquired a number of photographs taken at the mosque site by local journalists and this is one of them. It shows that mosque has been very heavily damaged. Parts of the walls, the roof, the minaret are all missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to new mosques and churches. Were they damaged to the same extent?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe what you're referring to -- and maybe we could go to the next slide. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I observed, as I also mentioned in my report, that in the areas that I surveyed ranging from Sanski Most in the west to Zvornik in the east, there were a number of mosques and churches that were still under construction on the eve of the war. Some of them were being used informally for overflow crowds on holidays, but they had not been officially inaugurated and registered with the civil authorities yet. In a number of cases there were old mosques and churches next to the newly built ones, and the old ones would be invariably destroyed or heavily damaged while the as yet unregistered, unfinished building usually had only minor damage. This is an example. This is the new mosque in Hrustovo-Kukavice in Sanski Most municipality. You can see there are two projectile impacts on the facade, but otherwise the mosque, its domes, is intact. Next to it at the right is the old mosque which we can see on the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. If we could have the next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the old mosque. This is a shot from the other side of the building. So you see there in the rear the rear facade of the new mosque. Next to it is the old mosque. It's completely burned out. On the right is a shot of the interior. I apologise for the quality. It is a bad colour Xerox of a photograph from a museum, but you can see that there is the prayer niche and the pulpit and especially on the pulpit you can see fire damage. This inside shot is immediately between the two windows at right on the inside of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the next slide, please. I think this is the next example.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a mosque being at Donji Krizevici at Zvornik municipality. As far as I'm aware, and as far as I was told by the Islamic community of Zvornik, this is the only mosque in Zvornik municipality out of more than 30 that survived the war relatively intact. Like the mosque in Sanski Most, it was under construction. It's very visibly a mosque. It has a finished dome, and behind it you can see the beginnings of a minaret under construction. It was clearly visible from the main highway leading from Zvornik and yet it suffered no damage other than graffiti and stolen building materials during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What conclusions, if any, do you draw from new -- newer mosques not receiving the same level of damage as the older mosques?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it indicates the fact that there must have been a pattern of going after the mosques that were actually registered. I hesitate to draw far reaching conclusion, that's really the Court's business, but I think it's significant that these mosques that were unregistered but otherwise highly visible were left untouched while the older ones were destroyed almost without exception.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've already surveyed religious libraries and archives of the Muslim and Catholic communities. There's two examples that you wish to show the Court. The next -- if we could have the next slide, please. What is the significance of this first example showing a drawing and a photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The drawing represents the town mosque in Bratunac. It was the headquarters of the Islamic Community in Bratunac municipality, and the reason I'm showing a drawing rather than a photograph is because the photographs taken before the war were taken long enough before the war that they don't show the little annex building to the left of the mosque. The annex building contained the chancery and the archives of the Islamic Community of Bratunac. The photo at the right is one that I took, and I believe what you're seeing there is part of the path that leads up between the mosque which is no longer there and the annex building which is no longer there. The entire site of the town mosque and of the Vakuf building, the endowment building that housed the offices is completely razed. This was taken in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could look at the next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This slide shows the town mosque and offices of the Islamic Community of Zvornik. It's in the centre of the marketplace in Zvornik, and the photo at left was taken just before the war. If you look to the left of the mosque is a large tree. This is a linden tree, sometimes known in British English as lime tree. In Bosnian it's known as "lipa," and it was a custom in Bosnia to plant linden trees next to the entrances of mosques. I point this out because in the photograph at the right you can see the linden tree. Again, we're looking at the mosque from 90 degrees clockwise. You see the linden tree with a deposit of garbage in front of it, and both the mosque and the small building that was next to it that housed the offices of the Islamic Community are gone. It had been used as a parking lot during and after the war. By the time I came in 2002, a court decision had compelled the municipal authorities to put a fence around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I want to deal now with what happened to the Muslim and Catholic religious and cultural sites after the buildings were destroyed. What -- what were their main uses of these areas?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated in some cases they were used as parking lots, as flea markets, very often as deposits for garbage. Sometimes junked automobiles would be piled on the site. In some cases there would be appropriation for other uses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go through the next three slides. First of all, what does this photograph show?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows another mosque in Zvornik, the Beksuja Dzamija. It was an old mosque in a residential neighbourhood and the mosque is completely gone. You can still see the linden tree. The pre-war photo is very old, but you can see the fragments of a wall and a huge dumpster full of garbage. This was in July, and the smell was rather overbearing. Right to the left of the scene is a large block of flats. So it was a rather odd place to keep the garbage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the next slide can be shown.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the third mosque in Zvornik. It is the Zamlaz mosque, and you can see it in the pre-war photo. To the right of it is a three-storey building with the characteristic striped pattern next to the windows. You can see that same building on the right of the photo at the right, which was taken in 2002, I believe. The mosque is gone and a block of flats and shops is under construction. This site has been appropriated and turned to commercial uses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Ms. Sutherland. Just, could -- oh, yes. This will do as well. A quick clarification. Probably I have -- I missed something yesterday. Does this number by any chance have any significance? Is it related to cross-reference to some other -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. In order assist the Chamber, Mr. Riedlmayer put the number of the formatted record for that particular mosque. So if you are going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, this is 22.31 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So if you go to Exhibit P4070, which is the formatted records, you will see the same pictures and all of the detail which comes from the survey database. And please correct me if I'm misstating this situation, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Formatted record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So we have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which we received in CD format.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, that is uploaded in e-court. What is on the CD-ROM is the survey database, because that is the -- the very, very large records of 381 sites, which is on a particular FileMaker software which is incompatible with e-court. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- that isn't in e-court but the formatted the records are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Mr. Riedlmayer, what's -- what's shown in this photograph, very quickly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is another Muslim house of worship in a village just outside of Zvornik. It's the shrine at Divic. The photo at left shows how it looked a couple of years before the war. They had just refurbished it and there was a worship ceremony. The photo at right is one that I took. You can see that the shrine has been razed to its foundations, and there is a truck, a lorry dumped on the far end of the foundation, which is where the tombs of the Muslim saints who founded this were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I want to go to the final two slides. Can you please describe what is shown in the first -- in the first slide?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a village mosque in Novoseoci Sokolac municipality. It's in the Romanija mountains north of Sarajevo. The photo at left is from the invitation to the opening of the mosque. It was rebuilt after having been destroyed in World War II, only in 1990, and at right you can see what the site of the mosque looked like after the war in September of 1992. According to information from the Islamic Community, the mosque was destroyed and the villagers driven out. Next slide. These are the remains of the mosque identified as such located at a municipal garbage dump at Ivan Polja about 6 kilometres away from the village. The remains of the mosque were dumped along with tonnes of municipal garbage, and in 2000 an exhumation was carried out on the site by the Institute For Missing Persons and found beneath the rubble of the mosque were the remains of more than 40 residents of Novoseoci who had last seen alive in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of those persons?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They -- it was a Muslim village, and they were Muslim residents, and they had been congregants of this mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes the slides. I would tender 65 ter number 23553, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4071, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, after you submitted your expert report, the survey database, and the formatted records, you provided two photographs which you wanted to submit as additional documentation for your expert report. These two photographs relate to sites 17.9 from the formatted records relating to Donja Puharska in the Prijedor municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Copies of these -- both of those photographs are already exhibits in this case, Exhibit P03564 and P03565. If we could have both of those brought up on the screen. Okay, this is P03564.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Would you like me to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reason I was pleased to get these two additional photographs which I obtained from the Islamic Community of Prijedor is that when I visited this particular site in 2002, the rubble had already been cleared and all that was left was bare foundations and the damaged house to the right of the mosque. These photos were taken in the late summer of 1992, I believe in September of 1992, and if one looks at them closely, first of all it becomes clear that this was a mosque. Immediately to the left of the house, the shiny white brick is the distinctive covering of the minaret of this mosque. This mosque was the first one in Prijedor municipality to be built with a dome and with this particular kind of modern covering on the minarets. Next slide.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Actually, before we move to the next slide, I need to correct the record. This is Exhibit P03565, I just see from the 65 ter number that I can see at the top of the screen. So if we could have Exhibit P03564 now, please. Which is 65 ter number 10978.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you have the scene from another angle, and you can see once again the covering of the minaret, and lying on the ground at the right is the conical top of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with those two exhibits. Mr. Riedlmayer in your report, expert report, in paragraphs 21 to 57, those paragraphs contain your findings. First of all, in relation to the Islamic religious sites, paragraph 26 of the report states that 266 of the 281 mosques surveyed were heavily damaged or destroyed, or put another way, 95 per cent of those buildings were heavily damaged or destroyed. Taking into account the dropped Schedule D sites, does this percentage change at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually did the calculation, and it changes it by less than half a per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think the -- the figures with the dropped sites, it becomes 226 of 239 mosques surveyed, with a total of 94.6 per cent. Is that -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Secondly, in relation to Roman Catholic sites, in paragraph 45 of the report you state that 32 of the 42 Catholic churches surveyed were heavily damaged or destroyed; or put another way, 76 per cent were heavily damaged or destroyed. Again, taking into account the dropped Schedule D sites, does this percentage change at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It changes but very minimally, by about 2 per cent, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with the new figures with the dropped sites is 26 of 42 Catholic churches surveyed where 74.3 per cent were heavily damaged or destroyed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you observe any other patterns with respect to the cultural destruction in the large number of sites you've researched?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The pattern of destruction pretty much cover the areas that had come under the control of Bosnian Serb forces in the municipalities that I surveyed. If one mapped the destroyed mosque sites, it was almost possible to draw a territorial map of what areas had been conquered by the Bosnian Serb forces. On the other side of that, there would be damage just beyond the confrontation line and only scattered damage elsewhere, but in the areas that were controlled by Bosnian Serb forces, there were virtually no mosques left intact. There's one famous example of an exception in a municipality that's outside of the scope of the survey, the village of Donja Baljvine in Mrkonjic Grad municipality, where local Serb residents stopped Serb paramilitaries from destroying the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Very well. Mr. Karadzic, before you begin, I have to mention that we continue to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis today as well, and I also note the absence of Mr. Robinson today for the record. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Riedlmayer, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I think that the cold air is still coming in, not directly at me, but I think it's more than necessary. Perhaps I'm just more sensitive because I am recovering, but I think this should not be happening in December. Perhaps we can arrange to have the overall temperature in the courtroom just a couple of degrees higher. So I would kindly ask for the Registry to see if the temperature can be a bit higher in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will look into the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, are you a scientist?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not -- not a scientist in that sense. I -- my education is in the social sciences and the humanities, not in the natural sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And during your schooling, did you ever take any exams in statistics?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what exactly is your profession?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm an art documentation specialist. This is what I've done for the last 26 years professionally. I have a degree from the school of library and information science, and as I published in the literature of the field, that is my principal profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were given the task, and this is something that you talk about in the first paragraph, that your task was to document the damage inflicted on cultural and religious sites in the communities of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, meaning Catholics, at least in 14 municipalities. So it was your assignment to document. Was it also your task to document only the Muslim and Croatian religious objects or sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received this assignment, like the previous reports I performed for other cases for this Tribunal, I asked for clarification as to whether I should cover only the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat related sites, or more generally, all cultural heritage, and I was informed that my task was to document the sites that related to the non-Serb communities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse the interruption, but Mr. Karadzic referred to 14 municipalities. I'm wondering what report he's reading. Mr. Riedlmayer's report deals with 22 municipalities, and I don't see it in paragraph 1 of that report in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Probably a mistake. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He may be referring to one -- one of the other six reports that Mr. Riedlmayer's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the destruction of the cultural heritage in Bosnia and Herzegovina, copyright 2003, Andras Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. That's another report. Perhaps the Krajisnik report or one of the others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's -- yes, quite likely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's possible, but I believe that the main things remain unchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you told thus not to investigate the damage on Serb religious and cultural heritage, and were you never called upon to testify in a case against Muslim and Croat military and political leaders?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told, as I just stated, to document the damage to the cultural and religious heritage of the non-Serb communities and the -- in the context of Bosnia, I did not testify against either Muslim or Croat military or political leaders. However, in the two other cases that I -- I'm sorry, the three other cases that I testified on Kosovo, I did include the Serb heritage. I was merely following the instructions that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you say that you received instructions from the Prosecution, and then you say the findings and the conclusions in these reports are those of the author. If I understood you correctly, the instructions were just as you stated them; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were part of the terms of reference of my mission. This is what I was asked to report on. I assume because these are the ones that relate to the charges in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were asked to find and to document buildings that are going to confirm the allegations contained in the indictment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it in that manner. I was asked to survey the state of the heritage of the non-Serb communities in these municipalities. It was not prescribed to me whether or not they would confirm or fail to confirm the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in lines 22 and 23 and 24 of page 17, that is precisely what you've said, that you assume that you were given the assignment based on the content of the indictment - is that correct? - and which in that case is in line with the requirements of the indictment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic is clearly reading from another report. I have a spare copy of the redacted version of Mr. Riedlmayer's report which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not refer to the transcript of today, page 17, lines 22 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My apologies. I don't know whether Mr. Karadzic wants this copy of the report that's actually in evidence at P4068.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to have one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I do have it in English, but I made my notes in the Serbian version, but I do have a copy in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Did this imply an investigation to be carried out about the perpetrators, the circumstances, and the intent? More precisely, what were you able to conclude beyond any reasonable doubt?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The questions of -- of reasonable doubt, I assume, are something for the Court to decide, as are questions of ultimate responsibility. What I was able to conclude was factual and statistical conclusions about the objects, about the buildings and institutions I was asked to report on. What my report does include is interviews with informants, some of whom refer to responsibility questions, but those are not from me. My interviews with them had to do largely with the question of when these objects were destroyed. The things that I was trying to exclude is either buildings that were destroyed before the war or after the war. Much of this investigation occurred several years after the incidents occurred, and therefore it was vital that I find out what the state of these buildings was at the conclusion of the war at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were able to establish beyond any reasonable doubt that something was demolished or knocked down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in a number of cases I was able, through observation, to establish how the building was destroyed, whether it was the result of blast or fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you an expert who could establish such matters, or did you have access to an expert who would be able to establish these matters?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not a trained arson investigator, and I'm not an expert in explosives. However, I would say that I've been at this now for more than a decade, and I have read the professional literature. I have visited and viewed well over a thousand destroyed buildings and have developed a degree of expertise in it. Most of my observations are based on simple common sense. If a building is missing its roof, the walls are charred, and there are bits of burned wood embedded in the masonry, it is an indication that there has been a fire. I don't think one needs to carry out scientific tests to establish that. If there are large holes in the walls and the missing masonry is cast at some distance, that, I think, is a clear sign of explosion, and one does not need to be a military expert. I was very careful in the language I used to refer to blast, because I'm not one to distinguish between different types of munition, but given those limitations, I think I can draw some useful conclusions from my observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you then establish the circumstances? For example, earlier we just saw the new mosque in Hrustovo. Did you know or do you know what was going on in Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not part of my investigation. I -- I was out there to establish facts about buildings, not about the whole context of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you did not determine whether fighting was going on at a particular location or not, and that photograph with a mortar hole is basically not explained, and it's not placed in context; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able in many instances to determine things like were there large numbers of bullet holes in a building or whether there were any kind of explosive holes in the building, but, no, I don't know whether or when there was a battle in the area or exactly what happened. I think that is ultimately something to be determined from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you did not establish anything in terms of the perpetrators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not my responsibility. The best I could do is establish the time when this happened, and I assume conclusions can be drawn from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say that something is demolished in Serbian territory, then the next step would be to say that this was demolished by the Serbs. Are you able to tell us which Serbs, or at least are you able to tell us whether this was the authorities or somebody else? Did you establish that it was the authorities that were behind these events?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, again, establishing responsibility is not my task as an expert. However, I can make the observation that, for example, in a number of places such as Prijedor, buildings were destroyed at a time when there was -- when the community was under full control of the Bosnian Serb authorities. I'm aware in general outlines of the history of the Bosnian war, so I'm aware of that much. I also know that in a number of locations the destruction of the buildings was carried out after the initial blast or fire by the municipal authorities using the equipment of the municipality to remove the rubble. So in that sense, yes, I can draw a certain limited number of conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that what you heard from the people, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That -- that is what I heard, and as in the example of Novoseoci, I think the facts speak to the removal of the rubble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you're not able to tell whether this was carried out, supported, or executed by the authorities or the paramilitary forces, am I correct then when I say that you were gathering evidence relating to civil war and not against Serbs? Because if that is the case, then I can support you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure I understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, rest assured that Mr. Riedlmayer has testified in relation to the fact itself. He didn't testify as to who is responsible at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, I am concerned about some conclusions and the manner of making the conclusions. For example, you say that new mosques were less damaged than the old ones, and your interpretation is that this is because the old mosques were registered. Is that the only interpretation, or is there some other possible interpretation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am open to other possible interpretations, but I haven't found one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you are knowledgeable about Islam and Islamic culture, do you know that mosques are barracks at the same time as well as recruitment centres and weapons ammunition and explosion depots as well as distribution points for weapons, and that these were mostly old mosques that were being used while new mosques were not in a position to be used for such purposes?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard any such thing, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For example, when a new mosque was opened in Kakanj in 1990, when the Imam says publicly in a speech that this will not only be a house of worship but also a barracks, you didn't notice things like that, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kakanj was not one of the municipalities that I covered, and I'm not aware of, you know, the contents of sermons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was in power in Baljvine? You said that this was an exception that you noted. You said that the authorities in Baljvine managed to dissuade the paramilitaries from destroying the mosque. Do you know who was in power at the time in Mrkonjic Grad and Baljvine.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I did not say that the authorities in Baljvine dissuaded the paramilitaries. It was Serb residents standing up for their neighbours. The information I have comes from a book by Svetlana Broz Croatia who interviewed the residents and included it in her book called: "Good People in an Evil Time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the police in Bijeljina, after the paramilitary forces members were arrested in 1992, interrogated them about who destroyed the mosque in Bijeljina and why this was done? There was also some talk about the copper from the mosque, and do you know that the police did carry out an investigation into that matter?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the investigation. However, I knew about what happened to the mosque in Bijeljina. In 1992, there was extensive vandalism to mosques, but no mosques were destroyed. The mosques in Bijeljina were destroyed in the spring of 1993 when Bijeljina was fully under control of the Bosnian Serb authorities, I believe, and there was no fighting in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also talked about Brcko and Bijeljina as being under the control of Bosnian Serb forces. Are you familiar with the way the authorities functioned in Bijeljina and Brcko, and are you aware of the efforts of the Serbian authorities to eliminate the paramilitary forces in those towns?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not part of my study.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, then you cannot say that they were fully under the control of the Serb forces, can you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is my background knowledge that at the time the mosques were destroyed that there was no fighting in the area. As I say, my field survey was not meant to investigate all the circumstances of -- of the destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, I'd like us to go back to the question of professionalism and objectivity. Are you interested in the outcome of this trial of mine?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am following it as I follow many of the trials at the Tribunal, but I am not here to judge you. That is the job of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, on the whole, do you have an interest in the outcome of proceedings against Serbs in Serbia? Are you a proper impartial witness?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a -- I don't have a specific interest that goes against the interests of Serbs. I do have an interest to see that justice is done, and whether it's Serbs or Muslims or Croats or Albanians, I hope that those who are responsible for crimes against humanity and other violations of international law will be prosecuted and punished, but I am no more in favour of sparing a non-Serb suspect than I am in sparing a Serb suspect, and anybody who is charged and turns out to be not proven guilty should be freed, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, until now, you were involved to a great degree in work against Serb structures. I believe that your lecture today also serves that purpose. So far have you been very active in presenting different variants of the Serb guilt? Have you been doing that throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, to go specifically to the subject of my lecture today, it deals with issues of post-war reconstruction. I don't see how that militates against Serb structures or anything else. I was putting the finishing touches on the lecture yesterday, and there are quite a bit of contents in there that are critical of both Muslims and Croats. The lecture is being delivered at the Meertens Institute of the Royal Dutch Academy of Sciences. It is not part of a political conspiracy of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not talking about a conspiracy. I'm talking about freelancers, as it were. Can you confirm that you wrote a short history of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the document to which you are referring. It was introduced already in the Milosevic case. It is not a formal publication. It was written in 1993 and posted on a web site. It is meant to be a short pamphlet. It's not part of my formal publication record. I tendered into evidence my CV -- or my CV's been tendered into evidence, and in there you will find my formal writings, and I would challenge you to find things in there that are anti-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: I'm not only interested in being anti -- in someone being anti-Serb, but also I'm interested in competence as such. Do you know what the social order was in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time of the Berlin Congress when Austro-Hungary was given the mandate to enter Bosnia? What social order was in place?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. As it happens, I wrote my senior thesis in college on that. It was many years ago, and it was mainly a work on diplomatic history, but I am aware that in the 1870s, in late Ottoman Bosnia, there were large landowners, and there were "kmets," the equivalent of serfs, who did not own land and who were badly exploited. I know what the social order was. I'm not sure, however, how that relates to my competence in writing an expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see 1D04902. That's that text. Let us summarise. So you agree in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time of the Berlin Congress feudalism was the social order of the day, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, feudalism is very specific to Western context, but, yes, it was definitely an inequitable distribution of land, and the vast majority of the people were exploited. This was in the 19th century. The same conditions in Russia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at the next page of this document, please. Do you agree that in Serbia already in 1804, in addition to this liberation movement, there was also a bourgeoise revolution that had been carried out?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the 19th century revolutions in the various Balkan countries all were a mixture of peasant revolts and the revolts of the merchant class. Karadjordje, the Serb leader who led the 1804 revolution, was himself a wealthy merchant. He was -- he had aspiration that came from his exposure to some of the ideas that were coming out of the French revolution and enlightenment, so -- but again, I don't know what the pertinence is to my report here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we shall see what it is, but I'm sure that you recall Leopold Ranke's well-known writings, especially a paper entitled: "The Serb Revolution of 1804"; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I read that. It was not part of my speciality, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at the second paragraph here where you say that Serbia in 1389 [In English] "... had suffered a humiliating defeat at the hands of the Turks at the famous battle of Kosovo and had been reduced to the status of an Ottoman vassal."

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know that at that point in time there was a draw, and France was celebrating the victory of a Christian army and that Serbia survived for another 100 years after that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now that we're back in the 14th century, yes, I know that at the end of the battle both the Serb leader and the Ottoman Sultan were dead and that Serbia did not completely disappear from the map for roughly another 70 or 80 years. However, during that period, it was a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire. I would remind you again, though, that what you are looking at here is a very informal history. It covers the Balkans from the late Roman times to 1993 in a total of about six and a half A4 pages without footnotes. So you can't expect to see elaborate details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Then we're going to abandon that. You also refer to King Tvrtko. Do you know that King Tvrtko was a Serb King?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour. Sorry, I've refrained from objecting, but really, what is the relevance of this to Mr. Riedlmayer's expert report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to page 3, paragraph 3. This is what you say there: [In English] "The Muslim Slavs saw no place for themselves in this proposed new order and continued to advocate the old Bosnian ideal of a pluralist multi-confessional society. For obvious reasons, the latter was also deorientation favoured by Austro-Hungarian authorities."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but unless this goes an issue relating to Mr. Riedlmayer, then I don't see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to show that Mr. Riedlmayer is an activist who is laying a foundation for condemning Serbs on each and every occasion. This paragraph shows that Mr. Riedlmayer believes that the feudal system in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where Christians did not have land or any rights whatsoever, was an ideal of a multi-ethnic and multi-religious society. However, that was slavery for Christians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how does it relate to his report? In this regard I need to correct what I have said earlier on. It's transcript page 22. I've forgot the lines. I said that Mr. Riedlmayer didn't testify as to who is responsible at all, but even if as a matter he may have done, however, what I meant was that the Chamber would not rely on Mr. Riedlmayer's evidence in finding who is responsible for destruction. This -- I don't see any point of going into this detail about the history of Serbia or Bosnia and Herzegovina, so let's come to the important points, relevant points, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I'm going to skip over all of those periods. However, what is of exceptional importance to me is to see whether this witness is impartial, whether he is a proper witness as such, so I would like us to see how Mr. Riedlmayer speaks about the Serbs during the course of the Second World War. Page 4, please, of this document, paragraph 3. Can we please have page 4, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph speaks about what Ustasha Croatia was, and what you say at the bottom of this paragraph is that as part of a short-lived all Muslim SS division -- you're probably talking about the Handzar Division. Do you know that that was the most cruel division of all and that they were there for two years?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the Handzar Division, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in the very next paragraph you equate Serbia and Croatia in the Second World War; is that right? You say that a similar campaign was carried on under General Nedic, who operated concentration camps for Jews, non-Serbs, and his Serb political opponents; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I'm -- by doing that, I'm not equating anything. I'm simply describing what I believe to be a matter of established fact. The Croatian regime under Pavelic had its own particular evils and so did Nedic. It is a fact that there were concentration camps operated by Nedic, and it is a fact that they persecuted Jews as well as Serbo opponents, and the fact is that they collaborated. Like General Petain in France, Nedic was obsessed with the fact that in World War I so much of Serbia's youth had been lost on battle fronts, and his collaboration in large part stemmed from that fear that this slaughter would be related. At the same time just like Petain, he had very right-wing opinions and in many ways sympathised with the far right and with the social ideas of the Nazis. So by saying that I'm not saying he was the same as Pavelic, but certainly both of them were, in their own manner, collaborators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, was this camp for Jews that was run by the Serb government, even that kind of government, Nedic's government, where was there a camp of that kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not the time for us to discuss those matters. Let's come to the issues that Mr. Riedlmayer discussed in his evidence in chief, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I kindly ask that we have a document shown. I really have to show how partial Mr. Riedlmayer is, how anti-Serb and partial he is, and these are dangerous things, and they are followed by bombs. First satinisation [as interpreted] and then bombs. And this is only the beginning. So Mr. Riedlmayer has an interest indeed in the outcome of these proceedings. I'm going to abandon this topic, but I would just like to see a document before that, 1D4922, to show that things like this are dangerous and highly detrimental and wrong. 1D4922.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Riedlmayer, that this is a map of the Yugoslav territories in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see a difference between Serbia and Croatia? Croatia is an independent state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't see any relevance in this document. Please move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, the camp that Mr. Riedlmayer is speaking of is in Belgrade, but it is in the State of Croatia. You see how far the Croatian state goes, and it is under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I said it's not relevant. Please move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this map be admitted simply so that the Trial Chamber can have it as such?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has given its ruling as to the relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a bit perplexed. How come I cannot challenge professionalism and credibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you challenging that the facts that certain mosques referred to by Mr. Riedlmayer were really destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm challenging are the implications stemming from certain conclusions made by Mr. Riedlmayer, implications that this has to do with the Serb authorities, an organised state, planning. First of all, I can prove what the foundation for such a basis -- what the basis for such a position is and then how and why it is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time, and the Chamber will have a -- take a break for half an hour and resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I return briefly to a matter the Court raised at the commencement of the session. I will raise it in general terms as the -- as the Chamber did. I am confident we are talking about the same matter, and I wish to advise the Chamber that the Prosecution has -- does not oppose the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the Chamber thinks that it should reassure you that the conclusions that could be drawn from the evidence of the witness as to Serb responsibility for the destruction of the mosques would not be considered by the Chamber. As the witness rightly said, the establishment of responsibility is not his task as an expert. The President said it before the break, but we think we should repeat it just so that you are fully apprised of the situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That you, Your Excellencies. Let me wrap up the issue of history with one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true, as the last paragraph purports to state, that you wrote that pamphlet with a view to having the embargo on the -- on arms for Muslims lifted?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you still referring to the document you displayed earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the short history of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please see the last paragraph, because I don't recall it. It's been many years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. 1D4902. Not -- a brief history.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 79. Last page, please. Not really. One less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph from the bottom. [In English] "Initiative to lift the arms embargo against Bosnia's government and call for forceful international intervention to end the conflict had been continually blocked in the UN and the other international forums." [Interpretation] Look at the entire paragraph where you speak in favour of the embargo being lifted; i.e., you oppose the positions of all those countries that would like the embargo to stay in place; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was based on my understanding of Article 51 of Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, which I believe I cite elsewhere here, which states that the right of self-defence of Member States is by no means denied until such a time as when the Security Council can establish peace and security. I'm paraphrasing, but that's the gist of it. And the fact is that in 1993 and subsequently, the Security Council did not succeed in its task of imposing peace and security, and therefore I believed at the time that the arms embargo was counter-productive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, it seems to me that this arises from your understanding of the interior structure of Bosnia. You say in several places that this is the territory under the occupation of the Bosnian Serbs. Do you not understand that the Bosnian Serbs were the population in Bosnia that was there for the longest period of time and which covered 65 per cent of the territory? In other words, they were not in a -- in another's country. They were in their own country, and who were they supposed to be defending themselves from? It was an internal conflict.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not here to argue the merits of the Bosnian war. There are a number of things in the question that I could take issue on, the figure of 65 per cent of the territory or the rather pointless argument of who was there first, but I don't see how this has a bearing to my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we'll go back to the report itself. I'll call up several documents which speak to the credibility and partiality, and I hope I'll have your leave to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In item 1 of your report, background to survey, you say: [In English] "During the conflict in 1992-1995, conflict in Bosnia, there were reports by various parties concerning the widespread destruction of cultural and religious heritage." [Interpretation] Therefore, there were also reports about the destruction of Serb buildings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that there is a link between the destruction of one set of buildings with that of the other set of buildings? Don't you see that there is some sort of a retaliatory nature? You did speak about that in the trial against President Milosevic. Do you make that connection, or do you believe this to be a state plan?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall from my testimony in the Milosevic case, I pointed out that there were definite instances of tit for tat destruction at specific times and specific places, but it was not the case in most of the municipalities. I can think, for example, of the early phase of the war along the Sava River in the north and south of Mostar in 1992 where you had precisely this kind of thing going on between Croat militias and Serb forces where, for example, in Mostar the two Catholic churches in Mostar were hit by the Serb forces during the 1992 siege, and after that Croat nationalists blew up the Serb cathedral and the old Orthodox church. Similarly, along the Sava River there were such things, and I would say I saw some traces of this during my survey, although it was not my task for the Tribunal to look at destruction of Serb churches. When I went to localities which had such signs, I recorded them because I was curious for my own research. So, for example, in Bukvik near Brcko there was a burned-out church. Finally in the very end stage of the war, in September/October of 1995, there were a number of Serb churches that were attacked in the western part of Bosnia. This is in Sanski Most municipality, mainly, and Kljuc municipality, where the Bosnian Army broke out of the Bihac pocket in the last weeks of the war, and at that point a number of Serb churches were burned, and I indeed have a collection of photos of those and plan to do something with them, but that was not part of my brief for this report. On the other hand, I would underline that in most places in Bosnia, the destruction was very one-sided, and I would also keep the time sequence in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you recall when Zitomislic as a very old monastery, I think dating back to the 16th century, when Zitomislic - which was a very important place for worship for the Serbs - when it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall it was destroyed in the early summer of 1992 by Croat forces. I actually wrote something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, you refer to the context, and that is a good thing. However, did you not notice certain patterns? For instance, you say that the Catholic churches in Western Bosnia and along the Sava were destroyed, and most of the destruction came about in 1991 before the war in Bosnia broke out, and in 1995. Did you notice that this was connected with the outbreak of the conflicts in Croatia and with the onset of refugees both in 1991 and in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, I would correct that the -- there was a very small amount of destruction in 1991 as the war in Croatia spilled over, but most of the destruction actually happened in 1992. The second wave of destruction happened in 1995, did coincide with the renewed outbreak of fighting in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In contrast to that, you observed, and rightly so, although I'm not sure your interpretation was correct, that the Catholic churches at Pale and along the Drina and Rogatica and at Cajnice, I believe, were not destroyed. Do you agree that this was the case because in that area there were no refugees arriving from Croatia; in other words, there was no fleeing from the Croats, and there were no refugees present whose churches had been destroyed in their native areas?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a two-part question, and I would like to answer part one first. I believe that the churches at Pale and Rogatica and Cajnice suffered only minor vandalism, in large part because there were hardly any Croats living in that area. In most places where attacks occurred, these occurred in the context of attacks against those communities, and in Cajnice, for example, I think there were no more than a handful of Croats living. The second part you asked about, the refugees, I'm not aware of to what extent refugees prayed -- played a role. As I said, I'm not in the business of tracking down individual perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would by no means blame it on the refugees. However, the influx of refugees does affect the mind-set and changes the climate, does it not? An influx of refugees with their tragic stories does have an impact on the mood in general. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just mentioned vandalism and the graffiti. Do you believe that it was the authorities who wrote the graffiti or whether it was done on their orders, and do you think that the emergence of graffiti in the world has anything in any way to do with the authorities? I'm referring to paragraph 42, although there are others where this is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I merely noted their presence. The vandalism as such could be quite extensive. For example, in the church in Pale, the saint statues were broken. The same thing was observed at the church in Brcko. In a number of other places, I believe that -- I don't believe it was the authorities that would have done such a thing. On the other hand, I believe it is the responsibility of authorities to prevent and punish such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 40, you speak of the removal of the rubble. Do you agree that it was in keeping with the rules of civilian protection that the debris that was the result of the general destruction in town should be removed and the public areas cleared up?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I won't comment on what the policy was or should have been. On the other hand, I do recall that both in Bijeljina and Banja Luka I've seen videos of how this was carried out. In Bijeljina, for example, you can see the old mosque in town being knocked down by bulldozers when it was still substantially standing, so I don't think it's merely a matter of public safety. It was, I believe, an active participation in the destruction. In a number of places, not only in that one village I mentioned, but in big cities, the rubble of the mosques was taken to the municipal refuse dump and buried under tonnes of garbage. Again, if the authorities had any respect for these monuments, they would merely remove the rubble and keep it somewhere to perhaps be used in reconstruction. So that's about as far as I can go in speculating about the authorities' actions just based on what I've collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But when you say that there was a case of a building apparently standing, don't you agree that it should be the expert on the statics that should calculate whether it was innocuous for the general public? Don't you think that it would have been up to them to decide the matter?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're veering into the realm of speculation, but I do have some experience with architecture, and the simple way of preventing an unstable building from hurting anybody is to put a fence around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if there is no chance of having a building reconstructed, would this not have been the reason to remove the rubble?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in many of these cases the buildings were listed monuments of historical importance. I would believe that in any orderly administration it would have been taken for granted that these sites would be preserved and studied for possible reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 31, you speak of the minarets that were damaged. Did you establish or did you have any sort of information to the effect that the mosques, and specifically minarets, were used as locations for machine-gun emplacements or nests?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific information to that effect. However, wherever minarets were still standing, I took careful note to see whether there were bullet holes in them or in the building, and one would expect that if there were battles going on around the building that small arms would be involved. Frankly, I'm not a military expert, but I would think that a minaret would make a very poor position for somebody with a machine-gun. It's a narrow staircase, and usually the balcony is very exposed. So I -- that's about as far as I want to go on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe, and, if so, what specifically with regard to blasts? You said that in most of the cases the explosives were placed within the interior, right, and that the explosions happened from within the interior of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I did not say that. I said that the explosives were placed inside the stairwell of the minaret, not inside the mosque. I am sure there are instances where mosques were blown up by explosives from within, but for the most part when you have a building like that, the signs are of, first, fire, and then blasts of the walls, and it's not the same thing as of the blowing up of the minarets. Very often the minarets would be felled in such a way that they would fall across the mosque and smash the walls and the roof. I have a number of examples of that. And I believe the point was the destruction of the mosque. It was not an accidental or coincidental thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because it is our position based on the information we got that some of the mosques contained weapons and explosives and, therefore, were destroyed as a result. In some cases the damage was extensive and inflicted on the adjacent structures. Were you able to observe anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again it's a two-part question. The first part that they contained weapons and explosives, I have not seen evidence of that, and I've certainly not seen any confirmed stories about that. In any case, I was not in a position to investigate that. As far as the damage being extensive and inflicted on the adjacent structures, one example is something I showed in court today, the Aladza mosque in Foca, where in 1996 still surrounding buildings had signs of damage from the blast, but I would note that the Aladza mosque in Foca was destroyed some months after the take-over of Foca by the VRS, and so it would amaze me to find that there were still Muslims harbouring weapons in a mosque in a town that was already under the control of their adversaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My position is somewhat different when it comes to the strength of the explosion. Do you know that, for instance, the Catholic church in Doboj, when it was destroyed a great many structures around it were destroyed in the process?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Catholic church in Doboj was annihilated by a blast. By the time I went to Doboj in 2002, there was no damage to be seen of surrounding houses, but I don't exclude that they existed. I did talk to the parish priest who recounted to me how it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is my thesis, Mr. Riedlmayer, that this was done by unprofessional, inept persons who laid out large amounts of explosives and in an unprofessional way. Do you agree with me that professionals would have gone about doing this differently?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a lot of assumptions, sir. I do know of accounts of destruction elsewhere which was carried out by professionals. For example, the mosques in Banja Luka which were all destroyed during curfew, and according to one account from an informant the Ferhadija mosque in Banja Luka was roped off before it was destroyed, and residents in neighbouring buildings were instructed to open their windows so they wouldn't break. So that would strike me as a more professional approach, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a single building which was destroyed in broad daylight and professionally, and do you know of any such heroes who would have boasted of having blown up structures, or was it, in fact, all done clandestinely and at night?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for a small number of instances, I have dates of destruction but not times of day. And that's all I can say with respect to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear of anyone boasting of having done as much or of being proud about it, or was that too concealed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did read a lengthy interview published in "Salam" magazine with someone who claimed to be part of a crew destroying a mosque in Prijedor and described how they had orders to do it. They arrived with their tools. They set to work. They put Black Sabbath on the mosque public announcement system, they took out anything that was movable, and then destroyed it. He seemed quite proud of it. I didn't include it in my reports because, first of all, it was an interview with someone with a pseudonym; and secondly, the building wasn't specified; but finally, also, because it had had no real bearing as to the specific monuments in my survey, but since you asked ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that hero spoke under a pseudonym, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm a bit puzzled by the statistics. For instance, you say out of 200 or I don't know how many mosques, 107 were damaged and a high percentage is stated. I'm just looking for it, but you do remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the statistics for this reason: Had you reviewed only what these 107 mosques, your hit would have been 100 per cent; right? Is it not a bit unusual to say out of such and such a number of those reviewed, there is a high percentage? Well, the percentage would even have been higher. In fact, it would have been higher had you gone and looked at only those 107, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your point, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to say that you chose 120, 107 of which were destroyed, and that's a high percentage, but in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see the passage first. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I was about to ask for a cite, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I will find this. The witness knows this, but I will find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, yes. Paragraph 26, I believe, sir, in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where you refer to 266 mosques.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of these 125.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Is this the passage you refer to, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this is something that recurs in several -- in several places. I think out of 120, 107 were found to be damaged, but this paragraph, too, states that out of such and such a number of inspected mosques, do you agree that that variable of inspected mosques is quite a flexible term and that it would be difficult to base a conclusion on something like that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you read my report carefully, you will see that I state in an earlier paragraph, and I'm sorry, I don't have the number in front of me, in most of the municipalities we went to, and I'm saying "we" because I had a driver, I managed to survey the great majority of the sites. In almost every municipality I was able to interview the local council of the Islamic Community or the local parish priest who then provide a list of the houses of worship in their area and offer to guide me to them. If there are intact mosques that I somehow missed I would be delighted to hear, but I don't think there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
