utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 14, you say that you toured 49 per cent of the localities, and you described 51 per cent on the basis of information from other sources; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a Serb guide who could also give you some information, or did you get your information exclusively from the religious communities that were affected?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I got information from a great variety of sources. I got it from the institute for the protection of monuments. As far as Serb sources go, in a number of municipalities I took great care to acquire cadastral -- extracts from the cadastral registers to make sure that the empty site I was looking at had been a mosque or a church. So I did not entirely rely on the religious communities. However, I must say that since they were the primary interested parties, they were, therefore, a particularly forthcoming source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 22, you even mention the period which is included in the indictment, and you say that no mosques were found that survived the war. You're talking about 15 per cent and only 5 per cent is being assessed as being only lightly damaged. Is this deliberate that you are referring to the period of the indictment or was this a slip on your part?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The period of the indictment was part of my terms of reference. I did, as I indicated earlier, make every effort to exclude buildings that had been damaged either before or after the war, but the active period is the period of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 23, you state that mosques with minarets are visible from afar. Are you able to say whether other locations, other buildings like mektebs, mejtefs are also visible from afar, even if they don't have these outside exterior visible attributes? Are they also easy to clearly define and classify by -- by their purpose just like mosques with minarets are?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, as I state in my report mektebs and mesjids, which often don't have minarets, had a lower rate of destruction than did the mosque with the minarets, and I assume that is in large part because they were not easy to identify from the outside. Where they were destroyed, I assume it was either because people went in or people had local knowledge, but I don't want to speculate. I cite examples of a number of these and they're in my database, and you're free to cite specifics and we can talk about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 31, you say that it was frequently said that all mosques in the territory controlled by Bosnian Serb forces during the war were completely destroyed, which is not always the case. You listed some municipalities where some buildings not knocked down. In that case could it be assumed, if we're talking about state policy, that people in those municipalities were disobeying the central authorities or that that perhaps was not a state policy at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't want to speculate about motives, but first of all I would like to correct something in your question. The point of paragraph 31 that I intended, at least, is to point out that not everything was completely levelled to the ground. "Razed" in English is not merely destroyed. It means the building no longer stands. It's my category "completely destroyed," there's nothing left. And there was a lot of hyperbole after the war where people exaggerated the extent of destruction. In fact, it was relatively uncommon for mosques in smaller villages to be completely levelled to the ground. It did happen. It was -- this was much more often seen in larger settlements. The sole place I know where the -- there is a report of the local population resisting an attempt to destroy a mosque is that village we talked about in Mrkonjic Grad, Baljvine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The mosque in Pale was not destroyed either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have access to my database. I believe it was a lightly damaged building, just vandalised but not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Novoseoci today. Do you know when the men from Novoseoci were died or were killed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when they were killed, but I did read testimony. I believe it was in the -- it's listed in my footnotes, it was either Brdjanin or Krajisnik, probably Krajisnik case, which says that they were last seen alive in September of 1992. I believe the story was, and Your Honours may have heard testimony about this already, so there's no point in me trying to summarise it, but as I recall the women and the men were separated. The women were forced to walk across the confrontation line to Sarajevo, and the men were not seen again until their bodies were discovered under the rubble of the mosque at the dump in Ivan Polja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also used transcripts - is that right? - when you were drafting your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to transcripts at several places. I did not use them extensively, but I did use them from when it was relevant to discussing a particular building such as, for example, Novoseoci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you were given the transcripts by the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not given the transcripts by anyone. I did what much of the public can do. I went to the Tribunal's web site and I used its search engine. It's available to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall the witnesses whose transcripts you used as a source of information?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I merely noted down the passage. I don't remember names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And to which municipalities did the transcripts refer?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one example I -- I remember is Novoseoci here but there may be others. Novoseoci is in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 55 you state that some scripts or the library in the old mosque in Janja were destroyed. Do you know that throughout the whole war Janja was inhabited only by Muslims and that they still live there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited Janja, and I talked to people there, which is how come I know as much as I do about the manuscripts that were destroyed there when the mosque was bulldozed. I also heard from the people I spoke with and in media accounts I read that there were expulsions of people from Janja during the war. There are, as I recall, three entries from my database that deal with Janja. The old mosque in Janja, the new mosque in Janja, and the archives and library of the Islamic Community in Janja, and all three of them were destroyed. I have extensive photographs. So -- including one photograph which was taken while the mosque -- the old mosque, the biggest mosque in town, was being bulldozed. So that helps establish how and when it was done. The photograph came with a date stamp. There was also published information about some of the manuscripts in Janja from a manuscript survey done before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will complete that with others. In the same paragraph you also refer to Kula Grad in Zvornik. Do you know that Kula Grad was in the hands of the Muslims for a long time, that they turned it into a front, they fired from there, and they could have and perhaps they did evacuate everything that they wanted to evacuate from there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that after the fall of Zvornik there was resistance in Kula Grad. I'm not aware of the exact history of the conflict in that particular area, and certainly I don't know of anything that was evacuated. What I can speak to are the three monuments in Kula Grad. One was the one you were referring to, the shrine of Hasan Kaimija, and I had -- I visited it. I also had extensive photographs from before, during, and after its destruction and reconstruction. And the second monument in Kula Grad was the Kula Grad mosque of which very little was left standing. It was destroyed by a blast. And the third one was the mosque of Avdo Tuhcic, which is on a hill top behind the -- Kula Grad and that, too, was badly damaged in the war and had to be reconstructed after. So that's what I can speak to specifically. I cannot really speak to what kind of fighting happened in that area. It's not what I'm reporting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at D1606 briefly. Who informed you about Kula Grad? Who was your guide?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My guide to Kula Grad was, I believe, the chief Imam of -- of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He did not inform you that there was an Orthodox church there and that it was no longer there at the time, and he did not inform you that Zvornik got its name after the church bell tower?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware of the story mainly because Branko Grujic, the wartime mayor of Zvornik, gave extensive interviews in which he spoke about the medieval Orthodox church that allegedly stood in the citadel and which he was hoping to rebuild. When I went to the citadel, there was already the beginnings of that with a bell tower set up, but the Orthodox church was not destroyed in this war. It disappeared centuries ago. So I don't know what the relevance is to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, it was frequently restored, and it was frequently knocked down. Did anybody inform you about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of its detailed building history, but do I know that it was not in existence in the late 20th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at this document which talks about combat actions from the Zvornik citadel and where a request is made to fire at the Kula because there were attacks and fire coming from the Kula and it was necessary to neutralise that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Your Honours, Kula Grad is actually the old Turkish citadel above Zvornik. Zvornik is on the riverbank of the Drina and goes up the hillside a ways, and then the old fortress, which is in a ruinous state, is on top of the mountain overlooking it. So it is a naturally defensible position. I accept that. The damage, however, the blown up mosque and the damage to the Hasan Kaimija shrine looked very extensive. It didn't look like it had been hit in any kind of crossfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you're not a military expert, are you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't claim to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 74 here, you talk about Mr. Besic's map, and I'm interested whether you explored also that side of our civil war, the hostility directed against religious symbols, or were you just looking for evidence of Serbian guilt?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly what was the question? How is the destruction of religious buildings a separate category from the destruction of religious symbols? I am not sure what you're aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question refers to this: Did you explore or investigate that received our civil war, or were you just looking for evidence of Serbian guilt?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we went through this territory already, where I discussed that the terms of reference for my survey had to do with the destruction of non-Serb cultural sites, that I nevertheless remain interested professionally and as a researcher in what happened to the cultural heritage of all communities in Bosnia, and, so, yes, I'm aware. I did not do a field survey for the Tribunal on it because I was not asked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you draft any texts about the damage of Serb religious and cultural heritage, incidentally? Did you ever publish anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I wrote a small essay on Zitomislic, and with respect to Serb heritage in Kosovo and now Bosnia, I've published a number of things. I've not yet published anything more detailed about damage to Serb cultural property in Bosnia, but it is my intention to include it in a more general account of cultural damage during the war, which I may work up into a web site or an article or perhaps even a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that perhaps I can create confusion here because I have a different text printed up, but I'm interested whether you'll stand by or abandon the assertion that monuments of major cultural and historic significance were intended for destruction. Did you establish that, and did you establish on whose intention they were to be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the major monuments, and here I'm referring to the ones that had actually been designated for legal protection within the former Yugoslav system, as I described, were damaged at a higher rate. Whether that speaks to intent or otherwise I will leave to the Court to decide, but it is a statistical fact. There were no world heritage sites in Bosnia before the war. There has been one added since then, the reconstructed bridge at Mostar, but, yes, there was cultural heritage of major significance destroyed such as the Aladza mosque, which apparently was under consideration for a designation for UNESCO protection. So the answer in short, yes, there were significant cultural losses and not just to the local communities and that the buildings of greater historical or cultural importance were disproportionally damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation for that? An example would be that older buildings are in more densely populated urban areas, perhaps, where the antagonisms are greater.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I showed at least one example of such a building, the mosque at Kuslat, which was certainly far from any urban area and virtually inaccessible. I can think of others such as the mosque at Ustikolina which is in a tiny village and was reputed to be the oldest mosque in Bosnia and was totally destroyed. So not necessarily. I think if one had to speculate about an explanation about why such things attracted more attention is perhaps because they were better known and, therefore, attractive in -- in the bad sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the Ustikolina mosque that you say is the oldest, when was that built?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was originally built in the late 15th century. Dates such as 1449 are mentioned, but it's likely that the actual structure that we have was erected later. It's been repaired a number of times over history. The most vulnerable elements of mosques are the minarets, which can be hit by lightning or damaged otherwise, and so they're the ones that are most often replaced. I've seen a picture of the mosque from the 19th century where it had a rather short wooden minaret and then it got a stone one again. So all of these buildings which are in continuous use are living structures, and the most you can say for many of them is that there is a known date of foundation, but only a percentage of the building is actually that old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking that because in paragraph 27, a mistake slipped that in the early 1400s --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 27. [In English] Close to half, 46 per cent of the 281 mosques surveyed for this report from the Ottoman era early 14 -- 1400s --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. What that designates is the era of Ottoman rule in Bosnia, not the era of the earliest mosque. The Ottomans entered Bosnia in the first decades of the 1400s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well at different times and at different years, the 1420s and 1430s they got involved in a local civil war among Bosnian nobles. Then they occupied part of the Drina valley. The last part of Bosnia to fall to Ottoman rule was in the north-western corner around Bihac, and that wasn't until almost a century after the first Turkish entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the time of the incursions is different from the time when Bosnia was actually mastered; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were already established Turkish administrations in Bosnia by the late 15th century. They didn't wait until Bihac fell to establish Ottoman rule in Bosnia. All I'm saying is that Bosnia did not fall at once. It fell in pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know -- or, rather, were you informed as to what the attitude of the authorities were -- was towards the destruction of buildings, any buildings, these included, that were in areas outside combat areas? Did you know about orders regarding protection, also the prosecution of perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of an order that was reprinted in a book called, "Moja Odbrana," "My Defence," which was published while you were still a fugitive. It dates from May of 1993, and it was produced by Mr. Milosevic during his trial. So I am aware of that one. I am not aware of prosecutions of persons responsible for destroying mosques and Catholic churches. However, I wait to be enlightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. D106, can we take a brief look at that. Let me ask you in the meantime. In what I have here, you said that the Serb authorities built a church in Divic. Do you agree that it's not the authorities that build churches, it is the believers that build churches?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The believers build churches if they have permits from the authorities. They don't build them at any spot that they don't own. And furthermore, at least in this case, I believe the authorities were brought to court by the Islamic Community and it was decided that the authorities were indeed at fault. This is a decision of the human rights chamber. However, it took years to enforce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the document that you meant when I ordered that patrols be reinforced and that places of worship be secured? That was in 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes. The 12 May 1993 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. D1736. Can we now have a look at that, please? Please take a look at this. The local authorities in Kljuc condemned over the radio what had happened, and they're talking about investigations and perpetrators, and this has to do with the destruction of the mosque, and you see when that happened at 3.00 at night, 3.05, as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a date on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that this is 1992. I cannot see the date. The 1st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With reference to the 12th May document, I think it's worth pointing out that at the time that document was issued in the aftermath of the destruction of the major mosque in the centre of Banja Luka, the Arnaudija and the Ferhadija, which were blown up on the -- around the 8th of May. What I recall, again from the Milosevic trial, is the fact that with respect to Banja Luka your order may have been issued, but there were other mosques in Banja Luka still standing at the time, and in the subsequent months they were destroyed one by one until in December there were none left standing, and so I was wondering about the effectiveness of such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I've been wondering that myself, but do you remember that I called that an act of terrorism, and I asked for it to be treated as terrorism?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the order speaks for itself without me having having to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at 65 ter 17851. Please take a look at this. This is the 23rd of June, General Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps is writing this. It's a military secret, official, keep permanently. He is issuing an order to make sure that no places of worship are desecrated. Also, fire may be opened on religious buildings only if the forces are being engaged from such building. Also, he is prohibiting the mistreatment of religious officials. Do you agree that this is an appropriate measure, an appropriate order issued by the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like the kind of order that would be issued by a responsible commander, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you minded to tender the Djeneral Jankovic's order which you showed --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that has already been admitted, D106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. It was yours, though. I was referring to 1D1606, related to Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that that had been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to turn to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is D1606.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. We'll admit this 1st Krajina Corps document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1979, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have a look at 65 ter 17848. Sorry, can we just have the next page? Actually, this one too. Can we see who all the addressees are? Oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this. On the 3rd of August yet again there is this order banning the destruction of religious buildings. "We warn all unit commanders to prevent such irresponsible acts. Failure to abide by my order represents a criminal act and shall be dealt with accordingly. " That is the 3rd of August. Can we have the next page now to see who this was sent to. It was sent, basically, to each and every unit. The first page it says "Military secret. Strictly confidential. Keep permanently." So it's not propaganda. It's not an act of propaganda. It is strictly confidential, it is a secret, and it is rather strict. So his first order dated the 23rd of June, obviously had not yielded fruit everywhere. Or rather, Mr. Riedlmayer, do you agree that a building can be destroyed by someone who is not in the military and that General Talic is not in charge of persons who are not under his command?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Again, it's a two-part question. Certainly a building can be destroyed by persons not in the military. And as to what the limit is of Talic's command responsibility, that I would leave up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit D1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now I have to deal with the question of your partiality. I do not do that happily, but I have to do it nevertheless. Is it correct that on various occasions you expressed your regret, for instance, because Serbia had not been found guilty of genocide in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a witness for the Bosnian side in the International Court of Justice, and in fact as I recall the ruling of the Court was that Serbia was in breach of the Genocide Convention for failing to prevent or punish genocide in Bosnia. As to your question of whether I had expressed regret, whether -- that the judgement didn't go further, I don't recall the specific instances, but I would agree that yes, I wished that the judgement had gone further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D4903. Can we have a look at that? It seems that it was at a very early stage that you took a very critical view of the United Nations and Western statesmen as well because of their understanding of the Bosnian crisis; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see the date, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1994. December 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. And this is the time when the Secretary-General was given an award at Harvard, and I made some critical statements where I'm quoted as saying: "The UN protection force cannot even act to protect itself, let alone ensure the protection of safe areas, the delivery of aid, or the position -- policing of weapons exclusion zones. "I think it's a very bad precedent to honour somebody for failing so conspicuously." I would stand by that quote, and I believe later on the Secretary-General himself had admitted that the United Nations had, indeed, failed in its mission in Bosnia. I don't think there's anything controversial about this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that this very same Secretary-General said that those protected areas had become armed strongholds of the Muslim army and that they had been abused?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that he said that, but he might very well have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D4905. Can we have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this. There was a petition circulated calling for the arrest of fugitives. I did not write the petition, but I am among the signatories. So are, I believe, thousands of other people. And if you look at the English or the Bosnian, you will see it says: "We, the undersigned, feel that it is the moral duty of our governments to order their troops in Bosnia to immediately arrest Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic who have been charged by the International War Crimes Tribunal at The Hague with genocide and crimes against humanity." Again, I think that is simply a statement of fact. The Tribunal did charge you and General Mladic, and it was the duty of Member States of the United Nations to execute the warrants of the Tribunal. I don't see anything prejudicial about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many such petitions have you signed altogether for other accused persons?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I -- I know I may have signed more than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose arrest? Do you know how many people were indicted here? Do you know how many people were fugitives? Whose arrest did you ask for?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously yours, sir, and Mr. Mladic. You were the two most prominent fugitives from the Tribunal for the longest of times. Most of the others were not on the run as long and were not a public issue in the same way that you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 9 of this document we can see your signature, so could we have a look, please. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last one before the fine print.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see it. It's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering the previous document as well about picketing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit both the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 1D4903 shall be given Exhibit D1981, and document 1D4905 shall be given Exhibit D1982. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4907. Can we have a look at that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have a co-operation with the Kosovo government, don't you, working on their independence, and you're working on cultural heritage in that context; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm engaged in something called the Kosovo Cultural Heritage Project which reconstructed some damaged cultural monuments in Kosovo. I was also engaged in aid to the Kosovo national library. It's all part of the public record. I had nothing to do with Kosovo's declaration of independence. And this interview with Dr. Shukriu was her thanking me for the engagement with reconstruction in Kosovo and with documenting the destruction in Kosovo. I would remind you that I also documented the destruction of Serb cultural heritage in Kosovo and was at various points in contact with the Serbian Orthodox church trying to work on Serb heritage in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This conversation took place within her preparations for the fourth round of technical talks with Serbia, right, as is stated here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what is stated is that, yeah, the first paragraph, that she was preparing for the fourth round. I did not participate in the negotiations at all. I happened to be in Kosovo on a very short visit of 48 hours, and I had an interview that lasted maybe 15 minutes which included snapping of pictures and the giving of thanks. It's -- if -- if I had been part of the negotiations, it would be a different deal. Most of my meetings in Kosovo had to do with the cultural heritage authorities who are using the database that I also submitted in the Milosevic case as one of the bases for their inventory of cultural heritage monuments in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit D1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the break, can we briefly look at 1D4909. It's a short document. This is translation from English, so the original should be somewhere. I'm going read it to you then. It says here: "Contact Washington. Let your voice be heard as well." And there's a reference here to -- actually, I'm going to read it out: "If we do not raise our voice in protest, that will mean that we are helping Western leaders get away with their new 'policy' towards Bosnia and ignore all --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you do not have the English translation, please let us know what this document is about first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an action over the internet aimed at supporting the Muslim side in Bosnia. It also contains Mr. Riedlmayer's letter to President Clinton, and that is what is important for me. That's on page 3. Can we move on to page 3 and that the gentleman, the witness, is going to recall that he did write this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Riedlmayer -- I'm sorry. Ms. Sutherland. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to say that there is this document in English, so if Your Honours were minded to rise early, then the Defence could get the English of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I think it's time to a break now. We'll break for half an hour and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For this session, the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the absence of Judge Morrison and Judge Lattanzi, who are away due to urgent personal reasons. Before -- no. Let's continue. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although I'd like Judge Lattanzi to be here so that I could wish her a pleasant upcoming holiday, still I can say that I will finish within a half hour. Can we look at 1D4909. Do we have the translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has it been uploaded?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't able to locate it, but clearly Mr. Riedlmayer wrote it in English. So it must have been the document from which the translation was done, but it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Defence can't locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you recognise it, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise it. I also recognise that there are some issues with the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 2 and then 3. Do you recall that this is a letter of yours addressed to President Clinton?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 3, and I'll read the relevant paragraph. I quote: "Lifting sanctions -- lifting the arms sanction would help persuade the aggressor that time is no longer on their side. The government of Bosnia, who has been internationally recognised, has agreed to every peace plan presented to them regardless of how painful or unfair it may have been. The extremists from Pale rejected every plan offered by the international community." Who was it that provided this sort of information to you, Mr. Riedlmayer? If I were to tell you that I agreed to four out of the five offered plans; whereas, the Muslims rejected the Cutileiro Plan which could have helped prevent the war, do you -- would you agree in that case that somebody must have grossly misinformed you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One question at a time. Let us stop here and then let us ask Mr. Riedlmayer to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. This was a very long time ago, Your Honour, and I'm working from memory, but at the time I was reading the news, and I was referring to plans like the Vance-Owen Plan, which was rejected. I would also, Your Honour, point out that over time all of us have opinions, engage in discourse of various sorts, including political discourse. I was writing this as a citizen of the United States to my elected representatives. That does not in itself render me incapable of writing a factual and objective and professional report. The views I held at that time - I think in those circumstances we're talking about the summer of 1995 - I think were appropriate to the times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the Muslim side had rejected the already accepted Lisbon agreement, as well as the nearly accepted Owen-Stoltenberg Plan?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my understanding, as far as my memory serves me, is that the Bosnian government at first hesitated then finally was pressured to accept the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, whereupon the Republika Srpska parliament turned it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the Lisbon agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Lisbon agreement came very early in these developments, and there are all kinds of controversies about why the Bosnian government refused to sign it. I no longer remember the exact details, but it was more than two years before this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me correct you, the Serbian parliament accepted the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, whereas the Bosnian or Muslim parliament rejected it. But let us look at this paragraph. So far UNPROFOR and the Contact Group have indeed become insignificant in the effort of arriving at the resolution of the conflict in Bosnia. The only thing that Karadzic and his highwaymen are still afraid of is that their victims may somehow find a way to get hold of defence assets or funds. First of all, do you know that my government at the time was among the highest educated governments in Europe at the time? Among them were various professors and highly qualified professionals from different walks of life.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the -- exactly the problem with the translation that I was referring to. My original text said -- referred to outlaws. Okay. "Outlaw" is a very specific term in English. It can be used in the broad sense to mean everything from highwaymen to bandits, but it also has the connotation of anyone who acts outside of the law. So you have things like outlaw governments and outlaw organisations. I would remind you, sir, that the Bosnian government was a member state of the United Nations. It enjoyed international recognition, whereas your government was -- had a Foreign Minister, but as far as I know was not recognised formally even by Serbia. And secondly, that it was in defiance of a long list of United Nations Resolutions. I would posit that it was acting outside of the law. All that being said, this was something specific to the period and long before I was ever asked to act as an expert witness for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Bosnian government can exist and be as such only if it is composed of the legitimate representatives of three peoples and not two and that we were that third part of the government?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we are not coming to that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One more question. Do you know that throughout the war the Muslim side in Bosnia did receive arms?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised, but it's -- it's not something that is within my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since I've read the portions, shall we leave it at that, or should I tender the document, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can admit it with the understanding that the English translation will be uploaded in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For safety, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the English original, Your Honour, not the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's not the English translation. It's the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you may recall since you sat on the Karadzic says that this same document was produced in the Karadzic case so the English one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You must be referring to Mr. Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant in the Milosevic case, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. No doubt the Prosecution will be able to locate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number would be D1984, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D4910.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You established, didn't you -- well, this is the same situation as with the previous document. This is a Serbian translation, and there is the Serbian original. You established an organisation called Bosnia Action Coalition, did you not? Or you were perhaps its member.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we don't have the translation -- do you recall that you gave an interview to this organisation then and that this is the interview we are looking at right now?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall -- do you have the date on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll look for it. There isn't one on the translation itself.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a vague recall of this because it was such a long time ago. I was interviewed about Dayton and its consequences, I believe. Is that the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have page 2. You spoke quite disparagingly of all the US politicians and Western European politicians. Power played a key role in discouraging the Clinton Administration from taking an active role.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: We don't have a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that? You referred to the Powell doctrine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Why don't we zoom it a bit further. Probably bottom half. For the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The part where it starts "In the course of the conflict..." Could we have the bottom two thirds enlarged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It reads here: "In the US, General Colin Powell, as the Chief of Joint Staff, played a key role in the Clinton Administration. 'To play a key role, we are dealing with deserts and not mountains,' General Powell insisted." You refer to this as the Powell doctrine. And further down you say: "President Clinton, already affected by General Powell's successful counter-attack in trying to allow the homosexuals to be in the army and unsure of his moral authority when it comes to the army, refused to --" In this particular paragraph, you are very critical of President Clinton, are you not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 8. Do you know, Mr. Riedlmayer, that the Serbs consider the Muslims to be the Serbs and that we are proud of the fact the greatest Muslim figures such as Mesa Selimovic and before him Hasan Rebac, Osman Djikic, et cetera, were Serbs? Do you know that we consider them to be Serb?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there are some Muslims who identify as Serbs. I also know that Serb nationalists insist that Muslims are as -- Serbs who have converted to Islam. Similarly, Croat nationalists insist that all Muslims are really Croats. I think what matters for people is what they think of themselves as being rather than what someone else chooses to insist that they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree, but we are proud of the fact that some of the most creative individuals of the Muslim faith preserved their Serb roots, but look at what you say here. How do you respond to the accusations that you're trying to simplify this conflict and present it as a conflict between the Serb bad guys and their helpless victims, and this is your answer: "This is a demeaning way of formulating the situation. First of all, this is not a conflict between a nation -- a victim and a aggressor nation. It is a conflict of ideologies. Serb nationalists, led by Karadzic, believe in a racial and ethnically pure state. To achieve this they expelled and killed all those who were deemed not to have been of thoroughbreds, of pure Serb blood. They considered it a crime for non-Serb individuals to marry with Serbs or have sexual relations with them, and such progeny of mixed marriages - 20 to 30 per cent of the people in Bosnia - were branded as half-castes who needed to be eliminated," et cetera. What prompted you to present such a position in this interview?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I would have to see the English to see whether it was exactly in these words. I would say that it is not a stand I would take today. It's simply the information I had then and the information I have now are not the same. Obviously this was an act of advocacy, and I own up to it at the time that's how I felt, but I would repeat once again that, you know, this has been a process of over two decades now, and in the process we all learn something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So would you agree that you did not see for yourself that there existed a single piece of legislation which was discriminatory, either in political or in racial terms, if I can put it that way, although we and the Muslims are of the same race, and in our view we are of the same ethnicity as well.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not familiar with the entire legislative corpus of your government. I know that the accusation made in this that mixed marriages were prohibited was wrong. It was based on misreporting. Since then I've learned that in fact, like all misreporting, this had some facts behind it, namely that people in mixed marriages were encouraged to emigrate, which is not the same, I admit, but this was the state of my knowledge at the time. As I recall, this was still before the end of the war, around October, while the negotiations were going on in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to tell you that in my office there were Muslims and individuals from Muslim families who enjoyed the highest of my trust, and if I told you that one of my closest associates came from a mixed marriage, would that shed any light or dissuade you from this misconception?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already told you that I -- I have retreated from this, disavowed that misconception of many years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If what I've read out is not sufficient for Their Honours, it may be admitted or I leave it in the hands of the Chamber, though I believe what the witness said is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification pending English translation likewise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1985, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D4923.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is titled "Spiritual Genocide." It is taken off the web site of the Serbian Orthodox Church. Can we have 8, 7, 5 -- page 7. I've called this up not because of the text but because of the images. Can we have the images enlarged, please. Does this look any better than what you've shown us, or does it look the same?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like a church that has been blown up. I'm aware of the book, and I'm aware of the pictures in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a basilica, as you can see. It was built in 1853. Can we have the bottom image now.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me read this out for you: "The church of the holy martyr of George, known as Donja Sopotnica, among the people, was built by Stejpan Herceg in 1446. Between 1529 and 1531, this --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what it's relevance of these questions and this material? Move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I wanted to show what the situation was like on the other side. This is a very old church, Stjepan Herceg --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. It is not one of his topics.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page just for a moment. I will not be reading out any of the text, but just let us look at what this was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we can 1D4924, and I'll tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. I will not allow that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not this document, but another document, 1D4924.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to your list, it says "Places of Orthodox Worship Damaged in Former Yugoslavia," which has nothing to do with this witness's evidence, Mr. Karadzic. Let's come to your last questions, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, it is my case that out -- that people fled these locations and that the chaos of the civil war encourages these developments in and of itself. So I am offering this not as tu quoque but as a way of giving you a better understanding of the motives behind certain events in a civil war and that certain events are not the result of the actions of authorities but happen in and of themselves. If you, however, do not wish to admit the document, I will withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is unanimous in that view. Please move on to your last topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, Excellencies, I could actually finish now. I would like to thank Mr. Riedlmayer. I would like to wish him a safe trip, and would I like to wish him happy holidays as well as happy holidays to the whole Chamber as well as to all the parties. I would like to wish everybody the best and my wishes for happy holidays.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have a few matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, this morning Mr. Karadzic said at transcript page 35: "Do you see that there is a link between the destruction of one set of buildings with that of the other set of buildings? Don't you see here that there is a retaliatory nature?" And then you provided an answer which included the fact that you said: "I would underline that in most places in Bosnia the destruction was very one-sided, and I would keep this time sequence in mind." Now, you recall the first slide that was shown this morning was of the Mutnik mosque in Kozarac and that's slide 11, P04071. While that's coming up, do you know what happened to the Serb Orthodox church in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it survived the war entirely intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So if we can just go to slide 11 to familiarise ourselves with what we saw this morning. And then if I could have Exhibit P00550.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is permitted, then I should be allowed to tender a document about the Serbian heritage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, is that the --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the old church in Kozarac, yes, the old Serbian church in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you know how far the distance between the Mutnik mosque and this mosque -- this church?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very far.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The second matter I wish to deal with is at transcript page 42 today, Mr. Karadzic asked you whether you knew of any heroes that would have boasted of having blown up structures. I want to play you a short video-clip of a speech given by the Drina Corps commander, General Milenko Zivanovic on the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this video is 65 ter number 40583, and the transcript of the excerpt that's going to be shown is from 65 ter number 03099 and it starts on page -- the bottom of page 16 and goes on to page 17. And the video is subtitled, Your Honour. And the time-code for the video is 00:38:34.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we stopped at -- the time code is 00:39:32.5.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, are you aware of whether any mosques were destroyed in Srebrenica after the town was taken by Bosnian Serb forces in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I covered Srebrenica for a previous trial, and I went to Srebrenica to do a survey. Srebrenica had a total of five mosques, all of which were destroyed after the town. You can see the intact minaret in the Petrovic video as the Serb troops come into the town, and then in the subsequent days you see pictures of several of them damaged or blown up, and by the time I got there all of them had been reduced to ruins. The one in the market square across from the Serbian church had been completely levelled and it had junked cars on top. The oldest mosque, the Bijela Dzamija, only had fragments of walls remaining. The same was true of the mosque at the northern entrance of Srebrenica and the headquarters of the Srebrenica Islamic Community at the Petric Mahala mosque, that mosque was completely destroyed. Only rubble remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Riedlmayer. All the destruction of cultural monument referred to in the indictment are limited to 1992; correct? In Schedule D.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there may be some dates in 1993 also.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to this. I asked --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is 1992, but it was in reference to a question that Mr. Karadzic put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this video relates to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like you to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I don't seek to admit the document -- the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, the third issue I want to take you to is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, if I can just correct the transcript. At page 76, line 15, the 65 ter number which I said was 40582 for the video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just state for the transcript that this was not prompted by my question. I asked about terrorists and General Zivanovic is talking about combat, about assault, and I was asking whether they were clandestinely or openly demolishing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's not helpful. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer at transcript page 55 today, Mr. Karadzic asked you if you were informed as to what the attitude of these authorities were towards the destruction of buildings, any buildings that were in areas outside combat areas. Do you recall anything said by Serb authorities in Prijedor about the destruction of buildings, religious buildings in particular?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall an interview by Simo Drljaca, who was the police chief of Prijedor and, I believe, had some authority over other parts of the Bosanska Krajina region, and he said with their mosques it's not enough to break the minarets. You've got to shake the foundation. That way they, meaning the Muslims, will leave and never come back. They cannot rebuild.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And finally, at transcript page 47, Mr. Karadzic put to you that the mosque in Pale was not destroyed either, and you just said that you didn't have access to your survey database. If Mr. Usher could -- or Ms. Usher, sorry, could assist. This is a hard copy printout of your survey database, and I've marked with a yellow Post-it Note the Pale municipality where it begins. If you could very quickly --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again I must -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- review your survey database records for Pale and inform --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not talking about the villages in the municipality of Pale. I was talking about the actual town of Pale. I know that all sorts of things happened in the villages, but I was talking about Pale the town itself where the Catholic church and the mosque remained intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, can you just confirm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- after reviewing your records, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's an entry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- for the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you hold on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since you didn't limit your question to the town specifically, we'll allow Ms. Sutherland to pursue that line of question. Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The entries for Pale are all for villages except for the Catholic church which is in the town. I didn't have specific information on the mosque in Pale. As you may recall from my database and from my report, I was careful to include only sites for which I had photographs and/or multiple corroborating information, but I have heard that the mosque in Pale was vandalised but not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the records in your survey database in relation to Pale?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I have several villages, Praca where the mosque was completely destroyed at site level. It was an old mosque dating from the 16th century. And mosques in villages such as Podvitez and Bogovici. And in the town of Pale, of course, the Catholic church, where the votive statues of saints on the main and side alters were smashed, but there was no structural damage to the church. So that's the limit of Pale municipality -- oh, no, here's also in Praca, next to the mosque that was destroyed, there was a mausoleum that was only lightly damaged. So that's the limit of the coverage for Pale of my survey. I must say that this request to cover Pale came in April of 2009 and I was not able to make site visits to these places, so all of this is based on photographic documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Riedlmayer. On behalf the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I'd like to thank you for your coming again to the Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, and thank you for making sure that I left in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I would like to thank you in particular for your indulgence. Please have a safe journey back home, and you may be excused now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter. The document D01736, the Kljuc radio document that Mr. Karadzic showed and you asked is there a date on the document -- Mr. Riedlmayer asked if there was a date on the document, and Mr. Karadzic said the 1st of July, 1992. In fact, the document is undated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have mentioned yesterday afternoon that the redacted report and redacted formatted records were uploaded and in e-court available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I have noted it. Thank you. Before we adjourn, Mr. Tieger, I was informed that the Chamber has received a courtesy copy about the motion for an extension of time for disclosure. Probably it will be of benefit to have the response from -- from the Defence. If you could orally explain it -- raise it now so that Mr. Karadzic could understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As the motion indicates, the Prosecution completed the searches and is prepared to -- as disclosed is prepared to disclose the relevant materials that resulted from the searches of the accessible databases and archives. During the course of that effort -- so in that sense as indicated in the motion we responded to and complied with the Trial Chamber's directive. During the course of doing so, however, we observed that there were references to certain documents that had not turned up in the search and considered the possibility that such documents may exist in locations that were not known to or accessible to the Prosecution, and therefore have proposed an additional search which would ensure the fullest possible compliance with the Trial Chamber's order and minimise the risk of any inadvertent oversight of materials that may exist. To do so, however, requires a labour intensive and time-consuming manual search, and then the scanning of documents for electronic searching. In light of those factors, we estimate that that additional process would not be completed until January 31st of next year and therefore seek an extension to complete that aspect of the proposed process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you follow?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, and I would prefer that Mr. Robinson deal with that, but we accepted that because there is no other way. There's no other solution. And then after that, hopefully we will get adequate time in order to be able to review that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The finding that this is -- request is reasonable, it is so granted, Mr. Tieger. Unless there are any other matters to be raised, the hearing is now adjourned, and we will resume -- one more. We will resume on the 10th January, Mr. Tieger, and on which date we will start with the videolink at 8.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have been working toward that particular date, Mr. President, and of course we'll advise the Chamber if there are any complications arising. We hope not and anticipate it would be on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm glad to hear that, because the 9th of January is Republika Srpska Republic Day, so I'm glad that we will not be in session on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wish everybody a very Happy New Year. We will see you next year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of January, 2012, at 8.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
